title: Cap. 7 Contra open: Obj. 1 — mercy vs justice in elect application
latin:
Contra haec omnia quae disputavimus de speciali intentione Christi morientis relata & restricta ad electos, & de salutifera applicatione mortis Christi ab eadem intentione dependente & dimanante, objici possunt.

1. Si in oblatione Christi detur talis intentio ad electos limitata, unde pro illis obtineatur efficacitas applicationis, & infallibilitas salutis, tum videmur illorum justificationem & salutem non tam ad eudokian, & specialem Dei misericordiam, quam ad rationem quandam justitiae revocare. Nam si quaeratur cur Petrus potius quam Judas gratiam efficacem & salutem ex merito mortis Christi acceperit, juxta nostram sententiam respondendum erit, Quia Christus speciali intentione & applicatione meritorum suorum id nomine Petri promeruit, quod pro Juda mereri noluit. Quod autem datur ex meritis Christi peculiariter applicatis huic personae, non videtur dari ex sola misericordia beneplaciti Divini, sed potius ex justitia: quia justum est ut quod Christus hisce aut illis personis promeruit, eisdem specialiter assignetur. Hoc autem videtur contravenire Apostolo, qui gratiam & salutem infallibilem praedestinatorum a pura Dei gratia arcessit.
pass_a_gloss:
Against all these things which we have disputed concerning the special intention of Christ dying, referred and restricted to the elect, and concerning the saving application of Christ's death depending on and flowing from that same intention, objections can be raised.

1. If in Christ's offering such an intention limited to the elect is granted, from which for them the efficacy of application and the infallibility of salvation are obtained, then we seem to recall their justification and salvation not so much to eudokia and God's special mercy as to a certain account of justice. For if it is asked why Peter rather than Judas received efficacious grace and salvation from the merit of Christ's death, according to our opinion it will have to be answered, Because Christ by special intention and application of his merits merited that in Peter's name which he was unwilling to merit for Judas. But what is given from Christ's merits peculiarly applied to this person does not seem to be given from the sole mercy of the Divine good pleasure, but rather from justice: because it is just that what Christ merited for these or those persons be specially assigned to the same. This however seems to run contrary to the Apostle, who fetches the grace and infallible salvation of the predestined from the pure grace of God.
pass_b:
Against all we have argued about Christ's special dying intention toward the elect, and about the saving application of his death that hangs on and flows from that intention, objections can be raised.

1. If Christ's offering carries an intention limited to the elect, and from it they receive efficacious application and sure salvation, then we seem to ground their justification and salvation less in God's eudokia and special mercy than in a kind of justice. Ask why Peter rather than Judas received efficacious grace and salvation from Christ's death, and on our view the answer must be: because by special intention and application of his merits Christ merited for Peter what he refused to merit for Judas. Yet what comes from Christ's merits peculiarly applied to one person seems to come not from bare mercy of Divine good pleasure, but from justice — for it is just that what Christ merited for these or those persons be specially assigned to them. That seems to clash with the Apostle, who traces the grace and sure salvation of the predestined to God's pure grace alone.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 1: mercy fulfilled through Christ's merits
latin: Nulla pugna est inter haec duo pronunciata, Deus justificat & salvat Petrum ex pura gratia sive mera sua eudokia, & Deus justificat & salvat Petrum intuens merita Christi pro Petri salute specialiter ordinata & acceptata. Ratio hujus rei in promptu est; nempe, Quod ipse Deus, qui ex mero suo beneplacito & pura misericordia decrevit dare Petro fidem & salutem, decrevit simul non aliter illi haec dare quam per & propter merita Christi Petro singulari quadam ratione destinata & donata, idque ex eadem eudokia & pura misericordia. Quae Dei eudokia opponitur meritis nostris; sed per merita Christi nobis applicata impletur, non evacuatur. Unde Apostolus Heb. xiii. 21. dicit ipsum Deum efficere in nobis beneplacitum suum per Jesum Christum. Quamvis igitur sit mera Dei eudokia, quod Deus velit Petrum efficaci gratia donare & salvare, tamen hujus beneplaciti executio non aliter fit quam per merita Christi. Huc igitur redit summa responsionis nostrae; Quamvis omne opus specialis gratiae quod fit in electis, fiat propter merita Christi specialiter illis applicata, tamen in illorum justificatione & salute veram rationem misericordiae, non justitiae conspici, quia Christus cum meritis suis, cum hoc ipso modo merendi, & offerendi sua merita speciali quodam intuitu habito ad electos, totum, inquam, hoc ex gratuita Dei erga illos voluntate duxit originem.
pass_a_gloss: There is no fight between these two pronouncements: God justifies and saves Peter from pure grace or his mere eudokia, and God justifies and saves Peter looking upon Christ's merits specially ordained and accepted for Peter's salvation. The reason of this matter is ready to hand; namely, That God himself, who from his mere good pleasure and pure mercy decreed to give Peter faith and salvation, decreed at the same time not to give these things to him otherwise than through and on account of Christ's merits destined and given to Peter by a certain singular reason, and that from the same eudokia and pure mercy. Which eudokia of God is opposed to our merits; but through Christ's merits applied to us it is fulfilled, not emptied. Whence the Apostle in Hebrews 13:21 says that God himself works in us his good pleasure through Jesus Christ. Although therefore it is God's mere eudokia that God wills to gift Peter with efficacious grace and to save him, yet the execution of this good pleasure does not happen otherwise than through Christ's merits. To this therefore the sum of our response returns; Although every work of special grace that is done in the elect happens on account of Christ's merits specially applied to them, yet in their justification and salvation the true account of mercy, not of justice, is seen, because Christ with his merits, with this very mode of meriting, and of offering his merits with a certain special regard had toward the elect, drew the whole of this, I say, from God's free will toward them as origin.
pass_b: These two claims do not clash: God justifies and saves Peter by pure grace — his mere eudokia — and God justifies and saves Peter with an eye to Christ's merits specially ordained and accepted for Peter's salvation. The reason is plain. The same God who, from bare good pleasure and pure mercy, decreed faith and salvation for Peter also decreed to give them only through and because of Christ's merits, destined and granted to Peter in a singular way — and that from the same eudokia and pure mercy. God's eudokia stands against our merits; yet through Christ's merits applied to us it is filled out, not voided. So the Apostle says (Hebrews 13:21) that God himself works his good pleasure in us through Jesus Christ. It is therefore mere Divine eudokia that God wills to give Peter efficacious grace and save him; still that good pleasure is carried out only through Christ's merits. Our whole answer comes to this: every work of special grace in the elect is for Christ's merits specially applied to them, yet their justification and salvation show true mercy, not justice — because Christ, with his merits and with this very way of meriting and offering them under a special regard for the elect, drew the whole plan from God's free will toward them.
